sections.title: Connection to yourself and the present moment

toc.title: Stopping can help build the vagal brake

blocks.p: We don't want to dive headfirst into meditation.
"We don't?"

No, we don't. If you tried to meditate directly on your stuck defensive state right now, it would likely result in overwhelm, panic, rage, or fear. Instead, we want to practice the smaller skills that eventually lead to unstucking through meditation. But before we even practice the skills, we need to understand when to start a meditation practice and when to stop it. Knowing both is a launching pad (starting point) and a parachute (stopping point).

Our general goal is unstucking. Absolutely. But unstucking is not the priority. Unstucking is a result of practicing the sequential meditative skills while grounded in safety. Those are the two priorities.

ol: Anchoring in safety and maintaining access.
Intentionally practicing the sequential meditation skills and making small improvements over time.

blocks.p: The priority in unstucking meditation is always safety. Not reliving past traumas. Not telling a trauma narrative. Not "sitting with it" when things are too much. Not triggering your defensive state and hoping for the best. Safety is always the priority: anchoring into it and deliberately checking to ensure we remain anchored.

When anchored in safety, we shift our focus to defensive activation only then. Instead of diving directly into shutdown, for example, you'll use the upcoming Skills Sequence, one after the other. Following the Skills Sequence ensures you won't get swallowed up by your defensive activation and that you always stay within your capacity.

You'll be better equipped to identify what is too much and to gently ease your way out of the practice. You have complete control over the sequential meditative process. As you practice a lighter skill, you'll determine what is too much or what else you can take on. If you can go further, you will simply use the next skill in the sequence.

Each skill will take you deeper into your inner experience and increase your potential for natural self-regulation. You don't have direct control over self-regulation, and you don't need to. You do have control over which skills you use, how much you practice them, and your progress through the Skill Sequence. So take comfort in what you can control and perhaps be open to what naturally comes from your efforts.
"Great, Justin. When do I start? How will I know I'm ready to practice the skills?" The simplest answer is that you'll start exploring your inner world through meditation when you feel safe enough.

But starting is more than just beginning. When I say "start" meditating, I also mean setting you up for success, beginning meditation from a place of safety, and ensuring you're adequately anchored in safety to continue. "Starting" refers to the setup, the beginning, and the continuance of the meditative process.

Starting should not be understood as forcing yourself through these processes. It does not involve diving into a stuck, defensive state before you feel ready. Starting does not mean skipping the foundational knowledge required for successful exploration. Instead, starting is a gradual, intentional process that allows for safe and effective progress.
You're not going to get unstuck in one sitting. You're going to come back to these practices again and again. As such, you'll have multiple "starts."

On the other hand, stopping means intentionally ending a meditative session when needed, rather than reflexively avoiding what arises from your inner world. It involves acknowledging what is happening within yourself, then saying, "It's time to stop." Stopping is recognizing the Polyvagal shift away from safety and deeper into defense. Stopping is ending a session with self-compassion and understanding, then returning when ready.

In essence, stopping is about pausing the experience rather than abruptly ending it. You'll stop when you're still anchored in your safety state, not when you spiral into dysregulation. (You'll stop then, too, but that's not the kind of stopping I'm referring to.) You'll ideally still have access to your safety anchors and prioritize your safety state even while taking a break from meditation.

Stopping does not mean things are hopeless. It does not mean you're failing. It does not mean you won't be able to meet your goals. It doesn't mean any of that at all. It simply means you're recognizing you're at a point where you need to pause. Or you need to stop and do something else, like a coping skill or a [safety anchoring practice](piece:safety-cues-and-anchors), then return to the skills sequence meditation when ready.

That's not failure. Instead, it may be a necessary step toward strengthening your vagal brake and improving your distress tolerance. You may feel discomfort or distress during the unstucking process. It's important to anchor yourself in safety and approach the experience with curiosity. When things become too much for you, that's okay. Tolerate what you can and stop. Anchor yourself in safety and come back to it when you're ready. Doing so successfully will help increase your vagal brake and distress tolerance.

Be mindful of your limits and avoid pushing yourself too far, as there is a risk of re-traumatization if you try to plow through the process before you're ready. Recognizing when to pause or stop can reduce this risk and make the meditative experience more effective.

Your stuck, defensive state will likely surface, or resurface, many times as you continue your journey and practice. The surfacing of the defensive state is not negative; it's a natural part of the self-regulation process. The key is to tolerate this experience with curiosity rather than allowing it to surface without invitation or welcome. Remain anchored in your safety state and come from curiosity as best you can. When you lose your anchor, it's time to stop.

The defensive experience must be permitted from safety to facilitate a shift out of your stuck state. Failure to maintain your safety state may result in dysregulation and re-traumatization. Likewise, engaging in reflexive behavioral adaptations to numb the experience only reinforces the stuck state.
For now, I want you to know how to recognize and normalize starting and stopping.

You know what starting means. Okay, great, but when do you actually start? When do you use the skills? When do you let yourself feel the defensive state, stay curious, and allow some self-regulation to happen? You already know it's when you have enough access to your safety state. But I want to take this to the next level and discuss two indicators that you have enough safety to start connecting with your defensive state.

blocks.h3: Connection to yourself and the present moment

blocks.p: You know what safety feels like now: calm, relaxed, connected, in awe, creative, playful, contented, and more. Safety takes many forms. When you experience your individual safety state, that's a good sign it might be time to start. But I want to narrow this down a little more. There's a specific flavor of safety we're looking for.

The safety you need in this first part is a general sense of connection to yourself and the present moment. This connection can feel many different ways, such as curiosity or confidence. If you can answer this question with a "yes," it's a good sign you have enough safety to start a meditation session: "Do you exist in the present moment?" If you can focus on your external sensory experience and natural breath with calm and curiosity, that's a yes to the question. If you have some level of awareness of your internal experience, that's also a yes to the question and a sign you're ready to move forward and use the skills.
But that's just the first piece.

The second piece is about asking yourself whether you can maintain access. Challenges will surface as you look inward. Old feelings and current painful ones will surface. I guarantee this is going to happen. We want to expect those and even welcome them. But only from a firm anchoring in safety. After anchoring, we need to ensure we maintain access. Only then do we go deeper into experiencing stuck defensive activation.

Anchoring in safety can take many forms: calm, relaxed, peace, playfulness, creativity, joy, and on and on. For this second piece, maintaining safety, we're looking for something more specific. If you feel something like one of these, you likely have enough safety to look deeper inward: curiosity or interest.

Why these emotions? When you feel curious or interested about something, don't you seek an answer? These emotions tell us you need to find something out. A journalist interested in political corruption will follow that interest to find it (which shouldn't be too difficult). An artist may wonder how to mix a specific blue hue and then experiment to find the right combination. And the Stucknaut, curious about their inner world, will follow that curiosity and discover what's inside.

Curiosity is the emotional portal to the inner world. I call this the Interest Impulse. When we feel these emotions, we have an impulse to seek an answer to satisfy our curiosity. I'm inviting you to act on your own Interest Impulse if you have one.
If you can answer any of these questions with a "yes," you're probably meeting the second safety criterion and have some level of Interest Impulse:

ul: Are you interested in what is happening within yourself?
Are you curious about your inner experience?
Are you open to what else you feel besides safety?

blocks.p: The Interest Impulse tells you it's time to take the next step. It does not tell you how far to go or how long to look inward. But it's a good indication of when to begin looking inward and when to continue. As you lose the Interest Impulse, it's a sign it may be time to pause meditation.

I met with Raul virtually. In our first session, he mentioned lingering "unease," anxiety, fear, and overwhelm. I asked if he was okay telling me more about these, and he politely declined, suggesting perhaps next time. I could feel his tension through the screen, his body and mind coming to a screeching halt at the idea of giving the uncomfortable emotions any attention. He completely lacked curiosity about these emotions. That's okay. It's to be expected, especially in such an early session, but I wanted to create a reference point for us. We focused on safety and set homework to increase it, too.

We met a week later, after he had successfully experienced safety every day, as planned. He connected with the breeze while parked at the beach, with the windows open. The next time he went, he sat on the sand and felt the ocean mist on his face. He mindfully enjoyed the warmth of his daily shower and even gave himself a few minutes of silence in the car before starting the morning drive to work.

During our second session, we practiced mindfully connecting with the safety experiences from the previous week. He said he scored 4 out of 5 on safety anchoring. I asked what he would like to do and offered him the option to connect with his defensive activation list from the week prior. He thought it over and said he was willing to. I asked, "Because you're curious or because you feel pressure to?" He said, "I'm curious." So we began the process of mindfully connecting with light defensive activation.

We first addressed anxiety, which he handled well and maintained safety access, hovering between 5 and 7 out of 10. Since he handled that well, we followed his Interest Impulse and permitted a bit of overwhelm to arise. That overwhelm connected to a few feelings, one of which was pressure. When we lightly touched on pressure, his safety state activation dropped to 3 out of 5, and we decided to stop there and process the experience.

The Interest Impulse happens in the present moment, but it's also connected to the next step. Your body wants to do something with that impulse. Compare this to the awe you feel when looking at a beautiful night sky full of stars. The experience of awe is a present-moment feeling of smallness and connection to the universe. But there is not necessarily an impulse about what to do next, except to remain in that present-moment experience.

But when feeling the Interest Impulse, it indicates that there is something to be curious about and that there is an action you can take on it, directed toward the thing you are curious about. It's happening in the present moment, but it's also inherently tied to an immediate future action. For our purposes, the near-future action is to look inward and begin the meditative process.

The Interest Impulse, like all impulses, is connected to what your body needs. When you feel curiosity from a place of safety and follow it mindfully, you're moving toward self-regulation. Mindfully acting on the impulse to look inward allows self-regulation to begin as your cognitions align with your inner world.
Self-regulation only happens if you are well-anchored in your safety state. Safety needs to have both pieces to it:

ul: Connection to yourself and the present moment ("Am I existing in the present moment?")
The Interest Impulse to carry you toward self-regulation ("Am I interested in what is happening within myself?")

blocks.p: If both safety pieces are present and you answer "yes" to both questions, it's time to start working toward your defensive state.

You can also ask yourself, "Do I feel too little, enough, or am I well anchored in my state of Polyvagal safety?" If it's too little, it's obviously not the time to start. If it's enough, you might start, but take it lightly. If you're well anchored, you can connect more directly with your defensive state.

If you're not ready yet, that's okay. Do the [safety-building work](piece:safety-cues-and-anchors). Become increasingly well-anchored. That's the priority you'll work from during unstucking. From the safety state, you can follow the Interest Impulse mindfully and have much more capacity to allow and experience defensive states.

If you want to assess your capacity for meditation more objectively, use a 0-5 scale to rate your current sense of safety anchoring. A "5" means you are well-anchored and ready to go. A "2" might indicate you are prepared for a lighter session, and a "0" anchoring in safety probably means you are in a crisis and should be using coping skills to get through it or seeking professional help. You can use this scale throughout a meditative session to gauge your continued readiness.

Yes, it's okay to think when you're meditating. Yes, it's okay to be objective about your safety anchoring. No, this doesn't last forever. Eventually, you won't need to use this level of objective thinking and will be more connected to emotion, sensation, and impulse. For now, if this is new or a struggle, let yourself be objective and use the 0-5 scale.

Knowing where to start is just as important as knowing when to start. I recommend starting in your [Passive Safety Environment](piece:anchor-environment), where you feel secure and surrounded by passive safety cues. This space will provide you with a constant stream of passive safety cues to mindfully connect with and anchor you more deeply in your safety state. From this safety anchor, you can then notice the Interest Impulse and follow it inward toward stuck defensive activation.

The environment is hugely important. Imagine trying to anchor into your safety state and mindfully connect with stuck defense while at work. What about at your kid's soccer practice? How about sitting in bumper-to-bumper traffic? Eventually, you will have so much safety and such a strong vagal brake that you can connect with a stuck defense in these environments. But probably not yet.

You can also use found Passive Safety Environments. These are places you don't control but have access to, like walking around a nearby lake or hanging out in a quiet corner of the local library. These are places where you feel safe and can easily connect with safety.

Natural environments are ideal for this, such as beaches and forests. Connecting with natural sensory inputs makes it easy to reach and maintain safety. But we don't need perfect natural environments. Parks and other natural-ish places can work well, too.

I recommend you immobilize yourself into stillness for the upcoming Skills Sequence. I find it allows for deeper inward exploration. However, this may terrify you. If so, feel free to mobilize. It's far better to walk around a local lake and practice these skills than to be immobilized in terror. As things get easier, try immobilizing more and more. Ultimately, listen to what feels safest for you right now. Your body will tell you.
"Justin, I'm scared I won't be able to maintain safety state access!"

That's a valid concern. You may not know whether you'll remain anchored in safety ten minutes after you begin. Maybe not even five minutes. Thirty seconds could pose a significant challenge for you! The good news is you don't need to know.

As long as you can access safety and recognize the Interest Impulse, you're ready to move to the next step. Remember, we aren't concerned with how long you're connected to the present moment. We're only concerned with your safety anchoring in the present moment, not with your safety anchoring in the future. As you feel it weaken in the present moment, you can decide to stop.
You'll consistently reassess your readiness as you look inward. Two ways to do so are to ask yourself where you are on your 0-5 safety scale and to ask yourself these two questions:

ul: Do I exist in the present moment?
Am I interested in what is happening within myself?

blocks.p: If the answers to those questions become a strong enough "no," then it's probably time to stop. Or if your scale drops to 2 out of 5. You don't need to know what your level of safety will be in the future. You need to know where it is in the present moment. If you're still anchored, then you continue. If you lose access to your safety state, then it's time to stop. Present, not future.

If you're scared of losing access to your safety state, congrats, you're normal! It's a common concern for those on this path. One more thing: I guarantee you will lose at least some access to safety. That's normal, too. We just want to recognize it as early as possible. The earlier we recognize that we're losing safety, the earlier we can choose to stop and recover.

blocks.why: Start in safety, every time. This practice is that first step.

blocks.p: How can you tell it's time to start meditating?

ul: What does it feel like to be grounded in safety?
What might the Interest Impulse look like for you?
What environment is best for you?
Is there anything you need to change about your Passive Safety Environment at this point?

blocks.p: Difficult Cognitions, Emotions, Sensations, and Impulses will surface as you follow the Interest Impulse inward. This is normal and expected. Still, it's important to stop sooner rather than later when things become overwhelming. This means you need to know when to stop.
If you are experiencing any of the following four signs, it may be a good indication that it is time to stop:

The first sign that it is time to stop meditating is intolerable distress. This occurs when the activation of your defensive state becomes too overwhelming, to the point that you are no longer inviting it and it feels like it is happening to you. Intolerable distress is a sure sign that the vagal brake has released too much and the safety state is not active enough.

Mindfully following your Interest Impulse will eventually lead you to your stuck, defensive state, and you may encounter many layers of defense as you work your way there. Ideally, defensive activation is identified, permitted, felt, and regulated through the skills sequence. Instead of feeling overwhelmed by the defensive activation, you will invite, allow, witness, and consciously experience it.

Examples of intolerable distress may include anxiety attacks, panic, rage, overwhelm, anger, numbness, fear, or dissociation. These experiences are clear indications that defensive state activation is excessive, and it's time to pause the practice, re-anchor in safety (or cope), and take a break from the work until you feel ready to continue.

The threshold for what feels too much varies from person to person. What is tolerable for you might be different from what is tolerable for the next person. For example, you may be able to invite numbness but not anger, whereas someone else may connect with anger just fine but not numbness.

Start with a tolerable emotion, then build your threshold from there. This gradual buildup is a sign of progress. While difficult emotions will likely come up, we don't want to start with those. We start with tolerable emotions, notice the intolerable, and choose to stop when necessary. Ideally, you'll notice these overwhelming experiences as early as possible, like catching numbness before it becomes a dysregulated shutdown with a dissociative episode, or catching anxiety before it turns into an anxiety attack.

Think about this in terms of the Polyvagal ladder. It's okay to drop down the ladder and experience defensive state activation. However, the safety state also needs to be active to tolerate the experience of accessing the lower rungs of your ladder. If we lose access to safety, we're left with raw defensive activation.

Another sign that it may be time to pause the process is when curiosity turns into evaluation. Curiosity is open and interested, while evaluation is judgmental and blaming. Curiosity arises from the Interest Impulse, eventually leading to self-regulation. In contrast, evaluation stems from increased defensive activation. Curiosity is open to what the present moment brings. Evaluation rejects it.

It's possible to notice evaluative thoughts and use them to your advantage by inquiring into what emotions are driving them. Ultimately, it comes down to what your safety state can allow. If you notice an evaluative thought spiraling into more and you can't connect with an emotion, that's a clear sign it's time to stop.
Let's get more specific with how these two potentials sound.

ul: Curiosity: "I wonder what's inside of me."
Evaluation: "What is wrong with me?"
Curiosity: "I wonder how I could improve this next time," or "That didn't work out as I hoped."
Evaluation: "I did that wrong," or "I knew this would fail."
Curiosity: "What's my internal experience of sadness?"
Evaluation: "How can I get rid of this wretched sadness?! I'm sick of it!"

blocks.p: If an evaluation is happening, you may have gone too far into defense, especially if you can't connect with the emotion driving it. It may be time to pause, re-anchor, and return later. If you can notice, be curious about, and be mindful of the underlying experiences behind your evaluative thoughts, that's fine too. If you can observe these evaluative thoughts popping into and out of your conscious awareness, that's a sign you're still anchored in safety and open to what is happening within.

Another sign it might be time to pause your inner exploration is losing mindful connection with your breath. But we need to distinguish between mindful connection with your breath and control of your breathing.

I don't recommend prescribed breathing techniques, as I'm sure you know by now. I'd prefer you mindfully connect with how your body naturally breathes. If you cannot connect with your body's natural breathing rhythm, that tells me you're not anchored enough. However, if you cannot control your breath, that is also clearly an indication that you have lost too much access to safety.

Think of controlled breathing as training wheels. Taking off the training wheels is a mindful connection with natural breath. Controlled breathing is typically used to manage emotion, whether to induce one or banish another. Your body knows how to breathe, and we're going to trust that. At least, eventually.

Keep our ideal meditative practice in mind: to connect with the present moment, whatever it brings. We accept the natural state of our body, including our breath. We don't reject it. As you connect with safety and defense, your breath will naturally adjust. I invite you to connect with it out of compassion and curiosity. Prescriptive breathing may thwart that effort.

Your body inherently knows how to breathe to meet its needs, not just at your baseline but also as defensive activation rises and your body attempts to shift state. Trust this wisdom. Think of your natural breathing rhythm as a skilled copilot during your meditation. While your conscious awareness is the pilot, focus may drift, or turbulence may hit. In those moments, the copilot knows how to keep things stable.

Disconnecting from your breath indicates that your cognitions are misaligned with your body's state or that the defensive activation has exceeded your current window of tolerance. It's time to pause and return when re-regulated.
The final indication that it's time to stop is the presence of intrusive cognitions. These thoughts, memories, images, or ideas enter your mind without your invitation or openness to them.

You may notice thoughts of shame or blame when you're in a dysregulated state. There may be images that disturb you. There might be memories you're not ready for that cause you more distress. These cognitions appear because they're attached to your defensive state. "Story follows state," remember?

The issue is not the cognitions but the state they arise from and the lack of safety. Ideally, you will compassionately notice the cognitions and connect with the felt experience of the state that drives them. You will eventually catch these thoughts, allow them, and tolerate them, along with the defensive state they come from.

Intrusive cognitions indicate that your defensive activation has reached the limits of your window of tolerance. If you cannot notice and be curious about these cognitions, that's okay. However, it's time to stop, re-anchor in safety, and return when ready.

blocks.h: Stopping can help build the vagal brake

blocks.p: Stopping does not mean you are weak or a failure. It does not mean you are a coward who is easily triggered and can't handle your feelings. Stopping is simply noticing when things are too much for your system and choosing to return when you are ready after re-regulating.

Just as a beginner in crocheting may struggle to get their stitches right at first, it's natural for anyone learning a new skill to struggle and not achieve the outcome they envision. However, with consistent practice, they can gradually improve and master the skill. Would you tell that beginning crocheter they're weak or a failure? Of course you wouldn't. Instead, you'd admire their intention to work on their craft and their dedicated practice, despite their frustration with not progressing faster in their crochet skills. You'd probably encourage and applaud their continued efforts. Let's apply this same standard to your efforts as well.

Unstucking is a new process that's probably radically different from anything you've tried. Instead of avoiding or trying to get rid of uncomfortable emotions, we're approaching them compassionately and gently. This is different. Very different.

Accept right now that you will repeatedly start and pause your meditation practice. Instead of imagining a smooth process, know that it will be frustrating and disappointing. You will have doubts and fears. You'll have moments of hope and enlightenment. Regardless, you'll continue through the Skills Sequence, noticing when you are ready to start and when it's wise to stop.

Just as our crocheting friend might stop in frustration, they will hopefully return to practice the next day, when they are more patient. In between, they might reflect on what went well and give themselves some credit. They may also reflect on what they can do better next time without judgment. As they continue this process, they build their skill level, and it becomes easier to do whatever crocheters do (this is the extent of my analogy, given my ignorance of the art of crochet).

I encourage you to do the same. As you decide to stop a meditation session, do something to anchor yourself in safety. Then reflect on what you accomplished and what you could do differently next time. Then try again when you are ready.

When you make the mindful decision to stop, you're creating a reference point for what is too much right now. As you continue to practice, you'll intentionally re-anchor in safety and then feel into that reference point with curiosity. Over time, you'll notice it's no longer too much, and you can sit with it while maintaining access to safety. Every time you practice, you'll notice the reference point shrinks or grows. Over time, you'll see a gradual increase in capacity.

Unstucking is an ongoing process. It's typically slow and clumsy. Yet it's essential for strengthening your vagal brake. Starting from a place of safety and stopping when necessary can build your distress tolerance. Your body will slowly release the stuck activation, and your safety state will strengthen as you repeatedly connect with the stuck defense. Your stuck defensive activation won't feel as scary. In time, you'll touch it with love and compassion as it continually softens and eventually fades away.
As you read the following story, I want you to identify when it's time for Paul to start meditating and when it's time for him to stop. I'll list the signs for your reference:
Time to start:

ol: Connection to self and the present moment

blocks.p: Time to stop:

Paul settled into his cozy chair in his dimly-lit home office. The hum of the outside world faded as he closed his eyes, tuning into the silence around him and settling into stillness. He gently brought his awareness to his breath, feeling the natural rise and fall in his belly, letting its rhythm guide him inward. Paul felt present and ready to follow the pull inward.

Initially, the sensations felt subtle: a light tingling in his fingertips, a soft flutter deep in his stomach. Paul met these sensations with gentle curiosity, acknowledging their presence. He wondered, "Okay, what's here right now?" inviting whatever was arising to be.

But as he stayed with his curiosity, the inner landscape began to change. The cozy settling in his belly faded. The tingling in his fingertips spread up his arms, feeling less like a flutter and more like static. He noticed his heart beating faster, a distinct thrum against his ribs. A knot formed, tightening in his chest, and his breath grew shallow, constricted, as if fighting unseen pressure.

He tried to hold onto his original open, curious stance, but his thoughts began to take a different turn. "Why is this so hard?" a voice inside him asked. "I should be past this. I can't believe I'm freezing up again. How can I have this much fear in me?!"

Paul tried to reconnect with his breath, seeking that calm, grounding rhythm. But it felt elusive, choppy. The easy cadence wasn't there; his connection to his body's natural breathing was lost amid the rising intensity. "Just breathe. Extend your exhale!"

Then images flickered behind his closed eyes - sharp fragments of old arguments, faces tight with anger, moments he reflexively tried to avoid. The present moment seemed to fade rapidly as fear overcame him. He couldn't escape the flooding memories.

Recognizing this clear and intense shift, Paul opened his eyes. He let the familiar room ground him. Placing a hand over his rapidly beating heart, he offered himself quiet reassurance, "Okay. Time to pause." He took a deeper breath into his chest and let it out more slowly. Paul got up from his couch, grabbed a coat, and went outside, listening to his body's need for movement.

"I'm not failing. It's just my limit right now. It's what I can handle now. I'm not happy with it, but it is what it is for now," he reassured himself. Paul walked briskly, drawing on the lingering sympathetic activation from his meditation attempt.

"I'm determined to try again after I settle down more. Instead of diving into the deeper sensations that led to fear, I'll spend more time with the settling in my belly I feel when I anchor into safety. If I'm still curious about what else is in me, I'll make sure to tiptoe into it."
How could you tell it was time for Paul to start?

ul: Connection to self and the present moment: Paul settled into the stillness mixed state. He brought awareness to his breath, connected with its natural rhythm, and noticed settling in his belly.
Interest Impulse: He felt a pull inward and invited whatever was within him to be experienced by saying, "Okay, what's here right now?"
Passive Safety Environment: Paul started his meditation in his office chair, using soft lighting.

blocks.p: How could you tell it was time for Paul to stop?

ul: Intolerable distress: Tingling turned to static, his heart beat faster, a knot tightened in his chest, his breathing became shallow and constricted, and fear eventually overcame him.

Curiosity becomes evaluation: His thoughts shifted from open curiosity to self-criticism and judgment, such as "Why is this so hard?" and "I should be past this. I can't believe I'm freezing up again."

Losing connection with your breath: He tried to reconnect with his breath, but it felt "elusive, choppy," and he felt he had lost his connection to its natural rhythm amid the intensity. He was also unable to control his breathing.
Intrusive cognitions: Unwanted images and memories ("sharp fragments of old arguments, faces tight with anger") flickered through his mind, and he couldn't escape the flood of memories.

blocks.p: Reflect on when it's time to stop.

ul: Which of the four signs are likely to occur?
Which of the four signs have occurred previously? How did you handle it then? How might you handle it now?
Which of the four signs are you most likely to miss, power through, or ignore?
How can you practice noticing it earlier?
